name: KolibriOS
summary: Free 32-bit operating system, extremely light, written entirely in x86 assembly, fitting on a 1.44 MB floppy disk and including a complete preemptive multitasking graphical interface.
license: Open Source (GNU General Public License v2 with components under BSD licences)

content.introduction: KolibriOS is a free graphical operating system for the 32-bit x86 architecture, programmed entirely in assembly language. Born in 2004 from a community split with MenuetOS (whose original 32-bit branch it continues and improves under open governance), KolibriOS aims to explore the ultimate limits of software optimisation. The complete system — including its kernel, device drivers, windowed graphical interface, a network stack and dozens of applications — fits entirely on a standard 1.44 MB floppy disk and starts in a few seconds on configurations with 12 MB of RAM.
content.what_is_it: Technically, KolibriOS is neither derived from Unix nor affiliated with Linux or Windows: it is a stand-alone system designed from scratch exclusively in x86 assembly for the FASM (Flat Assembler) compiler. Unlike modern systems whose successive software abstraction layers induce high memory consumption, KolibriOS interacts directly with the processor and the hardware registers with exceptional compactness and execution speed. The system is self-hosting, the integrated FASM compiler making it possible to modify and recompile any system component directly from KolibriOS.
content.kernel_architecture_preemption_and_memor: The KolibriOS kernel is a preemptive 32-bit monolithic kernel running in protected mode. It provides full hardware memory paging, isolating the address spaces of the various applications to prevent accidental corruption. The preemptive scheduler manages multithreading with priority levels, while the inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms rely on fast message queues and hardware event queues (keyboard, mouse, timer). System calls are unified and exposed to applications through the software interrupt `INT 0x40`.
content.security_and_privilege_separation:
KolibriOS divides privileges into two levels: applications run in ring 3, while the kernel and drivers share ring 0. Each process has its own page table and all applications are loaded at the same linear address, the `new_app_base` constant being 0 in the current "flat" kernel; the separation of address spaces therefore relies on page-table translation, and not on distinct load addresses.

The project documents the consequence of this model: an error in an application blocks only that application, whereas an error in a driver can bring down the entire system. The same page recommends using the application API, notably hardware functions 41 to 46 and 62, where that suffices, so as not to introduce code in ring 0; it also states that drivers cannot be debugged with `mtdbg`, which is reserved for applications.

Loading a driver goes through an interface version check: the `version` field encodes the native interface version in the low word and the minimum required version in the high word, the latter having to remain between the `DRV_COMPAT` and `DRV_CURRENT` constants. If the driver calls a function absent from the current kernel, the kernel refuses to load it and writes "unresolved" on the debug message board. This wiki page is flagged as deprecated and recent kernels use the PE format instead of MS COFF.

Data integrity is treated separately in the FAQ: FAT12 on floppy disk and FAT32 are read/write, NTFS writing is limited and without encryption, EXT2/3 writing is experimental and to be used with caution, XFS and CDFS are read-only.
content.filesystems_and_storage_capabilities: Despite its microscopic size, KolibriOS has impressive file system management. It provides full reading and writing on the FAT12, FAT16 and FAT32 formats, easing file exchanges with removable media (floppy disks, USB flash drives, memory cards). It also includes read-only drivers for the modern NTFS, Ext2, Ext3, Ext4, ISO 9660 (optical discs) and XFS file systems, making it possible to access data hosted on hard drives shared with Linux distributions or Windows installations.
content.graphical_interface_multimedia_and_appli: The KolibriOS user interface is a complete and responsive graphical desktop environment. It includes a taskbar with notification area, a start menu, a window manager with customisable visual skins, drag and drop and smooth rendering of vector fonts. The native software library supplied by default is remarkably extensive: text editor with syntax highlighting (TinyPad), image retouching software, multi-format image viewer (Kiv), video player (optimised port of MPlayer), audio players compatible with AC'97 and Intel High Definition Audio (HDA), PDF and DjVu file viewers, retro video games (DOOM, Quake, Minesweeper) and network utilities (WebView web browser, IRC client, FTP client).
content.hardware_support_and_boot_methods: KolibriOS runs on any x86-compatible microprocessor (Intel Pentium / i586 or later, as well as on 64-bit processors in 32-bit compatibility mode). It supports VESA 2.0 display as well as specific 2D acceleration drivers for certain Intel and AMD/ATI graphics controllers. The network stack supports several common Ethernet chips (Realtek RTL8139, RTL8169/8111, Intel PRO/1000) and partial USB 1.1/2.0 drivers allow keyboards, mice and storage media to be handled. KolibriOS can be booted from a 1.44 MB floppy disk, a LiveCD CD-ROM, a USB flash drive, a hard disk partition through GRUB/syslinux, or under DOS with the `mtldr` tool. It runs with perfect smoothness in all common hypervisors (QEMU, VirtualBox, Bochs, VMware).
content.history_and_independence: KolibriOS stems from a split with MenuetOS in 2004 and has since followed independent development, according to the presentation of the official site. The project was selected among the Google Summer of Code 2026 organisations and publishes a set of work topics accordingly. The two projects remain distinct: KolibriOS continues its own 32-bit branch with its own governance and repository, and must not be confused with MenuetOS.
content.system_requirements: The official site announces three hardware requirements: an i586 processor, 12 MB of RAM and a few megabytes of disk space. It also describes a boot from power-on to the graphical interface in a few seconds, with no visible intermediate step. These values concern the minimum configuration announced by the project; they do not prejudge the behaviour of heavier software such as browsers or media players.
content.download_channels_and_images: The download page offers four formats for version 0.7.7.0-9242, whose build is dated 18 October 2026: a floppy image (.img), a LiveCD image (.iso), a hybrid UEFI/BIOS image (.raw) and a .zip archive for manual installation on a USB flash drive or disk. SHA-256 checksums, previous versions and nightly builds are also published. The .raw image is presented as necessary for recent machines that boot only in UEFI.
content.documentation_and_community: The site is available in ten languages and gathers the forum, the wiki and access to the Git repository. The community channels listed in the footer are Telegram, Discord, Facebook, Reddit, Matrix and IRC, alongside an email mailing list. The online documentation remains essentially made up of the wiki and the pages of the site; no unified system manual is published on the portal.
advantages: Astonishing execution speed and responsiveness thanks to 100% programming in pure x86 assembly.
Extreme compactness: a complete system with graphical interface, network stack and applications fitting on a 1.44 MB floppy disk.
Minimal RAM consumption, starting and running with 12 MB of RAM.
Broad file system support (FAT in read/write, NTFS/Ext2/3/4 in read-only).
Self-hosted development environment with a FASM compiler integrated into the system.
Project under a free open-source licence (GNU GPLv2) guaranteeing permanent access to the source code.
disadvantages: Strictly x86 32-bit architecture that cannot easily be ported to other processor architectures (ARM, RISC-V).
Application ecosystem limited compared with the large operating systems with millions of programs.
Restricted modern hardware support (no native Wi-Fi, no modern Vulkan/DirectX 3D hardware acceleration).
Limited built-in web browsers unable to display contemporary complex web applications.
Not designed for enterprise server infrastructures or strict multi-user environments.
who_is_it_for: Assembly language programmers and enthusiasts wishing to study or create ultra-optimised software with FASM.
Users wishing to bring very old x86 personal computers with negligible hardware resources back to life.
Computer science teachers and students exploring the inner workings of x86 protected mode and of the INT 0x40 interrupt.
Enthusiasts of rescue or demonstration environments on a USB flash drive booting in a few seconds.
who_is_it_not_for: Users looking for a primary desktop system for modern web browsing or collaborative office work.
Developers depending on modern high-level software ecosystems (Node.js, Docker, JVM, Electron).
Modern video game players requiring recent graphics drivers and advanced 3D libraries.
Enterprises looking for solutions with guaranteed commercial support and formal compliance certifications.
content.verdict: KolibriOS is an operating system written in x86 assembly language. It includes a multitasking graphical system within the volume of a floppy disk and runs with minimal hardware requirements, which makes it a medium for studying compact systems.
content.release_history_and_nightly_build_number:
The project archives its versions on archive.kolibrios.org. The page consulted on 2026-10-18 lists version 0.7.7.0 on 13 December 2009, presented as a recent version, then 0.7.5.0 on 31 January 2009, 0.7.1.0 on 23 September 2007 and 0.7.0.0 on 7 June 2007. For each version, the archive publishes a floppy image, a CD image (LiveCD), the source code as of the version date and a development kit (SDK).

The current images are not stable releases: the download page presents them as nightly builds that contain the most recent changes and may therefore be unstable, and the files are compressed in 7zip. Their number repeats the stable version and extends it with a build number and a suffix: during the consultation of 18 October 2026, the page displayed 0.7.7.0-9244-gb6ad1799 with the build date 18/10/2026. The entry also notes the build 0.7.7.0-9242, dated the same day; the two numbers differ, the displayed date is identical.

The build server builds.kolibrios.org publishes the images per language, with the directories en_US, es_ES, et_EE, it_IT and ru_RU, in a ci/ directory, alongside the docs/ and doxygen/ directories and files such as active_devs.txt; the index consulted lists eight directories and three files.

These pages publish neither a stable release schedule, nor a support period, nor an end-of-life date for the 0.7.7.0 series.
